title: The Copper Lantern
premise: In 1898, Beatrix Underhill, daughter of a drowned pearl diver and indentured to the Meridian Trading Company, has spent nine years keeping her head down in the company's coastal workshop, mending nets and copying ledgers. When the colonial army requisitions the town for war, they seize the master ledger containing every indentured worker's name—including hers—and plan to burn the records along with the debts owed to them. Discovering that her late mother's name appears in the ledger's oldest pages with an unpaid inheritance of pearl rights, Beatrix realizes the document is both her prison and her legacy. With the help of the workshop's found family—a one-handed sailmaker, a deaf cook, and the foreman who secretly taught her to read—she races to copy the ledger before the army's torches arrive. In the end, she delivers the copied names to the magistrate, wins freedom for herself and the others, and claims her mother's inheritance, choosing to stay not as property but as family.
about_author: Elodie Ashgrove is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing maritime trade records from the late nineteenth century. She writes historical fiction about the people whose names were recorded only as entries in ledgers.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. We meet her in the rhythm of workshop life: diving for salvage at dawn, copying figures by lamplight, invisible among forty indentured workers. The copper lantern her mother left her hangs unlit over her cot. When soldiers march into town posting requisition notices, the foreman quietly warns her the company's papers are 'coming due.' Emotional beat: uneasy belonging—she loves this place that owns her.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Ordered to prepare the archives for destruction, she discovers her mother's entry: pearl rights never claimed, a debt marked paid with a single dive. The sailmaker, Tam, reveals he helped her mother once and owes her a debt of his own. As army officers inventory the town, Beatrix begins memorizing names at night. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose; invisibility becomes a weapon.

chapters.title: Nine Nights of Copper Light
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, with interludes from the deaf cook Marta's perspective. The found family works in secret: Tam distracts the garrison, Marta hides copied pages in flour sacks, the foreman falsifies the burn schedule to buy time. A young officer grows suspicious of the lantern burning late each night. On the ninth night he catches Beatrix mid-copy—and instead of reporting her, asks her to add his sister's name, sold to the same company years ago. Emotional beat: terror giving way to solidarity.

chapters.title: The Burning and the Keeping
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The army arrives early to torch the workshop. As flames take the rafters, Beatrix, Tam, Marta, and the officer smuggle the full copied ledger out through the smoke to the magistrate across the bay. Debts voided, names restored, Beatrix lights her mother's copper lantern at last and hangs it in the rebuilt workshop door—not for the company, but for everyone who will come after. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed; belonging chosen, not assigned.
